title.zh: 爭水即爭地：墨西哥城街頭居民如何以一場井水之戰守住家園
title.en: Fighting for Water Is Fighting for Home: How a Mexico City Neighborhood Defended Its Place One Well at a Time

summary.zh:
【總結】本文以墨西哥城南部的聖多明哥（Santo Domingo）社區為案例，揭示在貧民社區中，「捍衛水源」本質上就是「捍衛家園」。居民因自來水供應時斷時續、配水被政治人物操縱為收買選票的工具，於二零二零年成立「水權守護委員會」，爭取一口直接連入管網的新水井。研究指出，這項行動不只是爭取飲用水，而是透過降低生活不確定性、打破恩庇政治、以及為社區想像未來三條途徑，將水資源之爭轉化為對「在此安居權利」的抗爭。此發現填補了過去研究忽視「水資源不安全如何成為緩慢驅離力量」的盲點，也為城市政治生態學與基礎設施公民權的討論提供了新的經驗基礎。

【研究問題】過去關於水資源的研究多聚焦於家庭層面的應對策略，或將水權鬥爭簡化為「國家敵人／夥伴」的二元框架，卻較少回答：在自建成份濃厚的社區裡，水資源不安全如何成為一種「緩慢驅離」（displacement without moving）的力量？為什麼理解這一點至關重要？因為當配水被政治人物武器化，居民不僅承受日常苦難，更被迫在「投票換水」與「斷水」之間抉擇，社區的存续因此受到威脅。本文正是要揭示水資源鬥爭如何同時是空間、政治與身分的鬥爭。

【研究方法】作者於二零二至二零二三年間在墨西哥城進行田野調查，以聖多明哥社區的「水權守護委員會」為單一案例，採用定性研究設計。資料來源包括二十二場深度訪談、十一本參與者日記（記錄每日來水狀況與情緒反應）、八場邊走邊訪的移動式訪談，以及對集會與街頭活動的參與觀察。所有訪談以西班牙語進行，之後轉錄並翻譯為英文。資料分析採用主題分析法，歸納出「焦慮、苦難、政治操弄、未來期待」四大核心主題；並輔以敘事分析，追蹤同一參與者在不同時點如何串連這些主題。研究對象皆為委員會成員，以化名保護隱私，社區與組織名稱則予以保留。

【結果】研究歸納出三項相互關聯的機制。第一，降低不確定性：水井通水後，居民從「整天等水車、神經緊繃」轉為「敢於洗衣打掃、安心生活」，一位參與者日記寫道：「今天開水龍頭，水壓很好，我很開心。」第二，對抗恩庇政治：過去水車分配成為政治人物的籌碼，「不投給我就沒水」；新井連入管網後，居民對水車的依賴下降，政治綁架被削弱。第三，塑造社區未來：長者將社區視為「幾代人用勞力建起來的家」，擔憂房地產開發與地下水超抽會將他們逐步驅離；水井之爭因此成為對抗「強制遷離」的抗爭。研究指出，捍衛水源即捍衛在社區中繼續生活的權利，這也為全球南方快速城市化的貧民社區提供了理解基礎設施抗爭的新框架。
summary.en:
**Summary:** This article examines how water defense in a popular neighborhood becomes place defense. Focusing on the Water Defence Committee of Santo Domingo in southern Mexico City, it shows that residents' struggle for a new well connected to the public pipe network was never just about access to a resource. It was about reducing the chronic uncertainty of intermittent supply, breaking the clientelist grip of politicians who weaponized water truck deliveries, and securing the material conditions for remaining in a neighborhood built through generations of collective labor. The study fills a gap in urban political ecology by conceptualizing water insecurity as a slow, politically produced force of displacement, and by showing how everyday water struggles reconfigure citizenship in tension with the state.

**Problem:** Previous research on water insecurity has largely focused on household-level coping strategies or framed water struggles as either state-dominated or fully autonomous. What has been missing is an understanding of how water insecurity operates as a displacing force in self-built neighborhoods, and how defending water becomes defending the right to stay. This matters because in cities across the Global South, unreliable infrastructure and political manipulation of services threaten not just comfort but the very possibility of remaining in place. Without this lens, water conflicts are reduced to technical grievances rather than recognized as struggles over urban survival and belonging.

**Approach:** The author conducted qualitative fieldwork in Mexico City between 2022 and 2023, centering on the Water Defence Committee of Santo Domingo (WDC), a resident-led organization formed in early 2020. Data came from twenty-two in-depth interviews, eleven participant diaries recording daily water availability and emotional responses over two weeks, eight walking interviews where residents led the researcher through the neighborhood, and participant observation at assemblies and street events. All interviews were conducted in Spanish, transcribed, and translated. Thematic analysis identified recurring patterns around anxiety, suffering, political manipulation, and future expectations, while narrative analysis traced how individual participants connected these themes across time. All participants were WDC members; names were pseudonymized.

**Results:** Three interrelated mechanisms emerged. First, reducing uncertainty: the new well, operational by late 2022, transformed daily life from constant tension to relative calm. One participant wrote in her diary, "I open the tap and realize the water comes with very good pressure—today we can clean and wash without fear." Second, confronting clientelism: water trucks had been used by politicians as political spoils, with explicit quid-pro-quo demands. The well, fed directly by the public network, reduced dependence on discretionary truck deliveries and weakened this leverage. Third, shaping the future: residents framed the neighborhood as an intergenerational project built through collective labor, and saw water insecurity as linked to broader pressures from real estate development and aquifer depletion that threatened gradual displacement. One elder warned, "We are being pushed aside little by little. Because of this scarcity, we will have to look for another place to live." The study demonstrates that water defense in popular neighborhoods is simultaneously a defense of place, citizenship, and the right to remain.

keyArticle.title: Defending water, defending place: Water insecurity and neighbour-based organising in Mexico City's popular neighbourhoods
